column1: # manifest.tsv — the unredaction bench's real-world documents (#1591, bench #1590).
# WHAT IS IN GIT AND WHAT IS NOT
# THIS FILE is tracked: ids, URLs, hashes and the VETTING RECORD.
# The PDFs are not — they land in test-pdfs/unredaction-bench/, gitignored.
# The recovered or published VALUES are not, anywhere, ever. There is no column
# for them and UnredactionBenchManifestTests fails if one is added (#1602).
# Ground truth for tier B lives in a gitignored local file built by hand:
#   test-pdfs/unredaction-bench/ground-truth.local.tsv
# so the repository never republishes text a court or an agency tried to
# withhold, even where a newspaper already has.
# COLUMNS (tab-separated)
#   id            stable slug; also the local filename stem
#   tier          B — the hidden value is already published, so the bench can SCORE
#                 C — public record, no published ground truth; leak CLASS only, never values
#                 D — sensitive-provenance sources under a value-free positional design (#1603)
#   status        vetted   — all three vetting questions answered yes; the script downloads it
#                 excluded — assessed and REJECTED; never downloaded. The reason is the point.
#                 blocked  — assessed, WANTED, and cannot be fetched by this script. Not a
#                            rejection and not an oversight: something outside the vetting
#                            questions is in the way (a bot wall that refuses every
#                            self-identifying User-Agent, a source with no durable URL). The
#                            row says what the obstacle is so a human can clear it or fetch
#                            the file by hand.
#                 unvetted — recorded so the next reader knows it exists and that NOBODY HAS
#                            LOOKED YET. Not downloaded.
#                 These four are deliberately distinct. "We checked and it is fine", "we
#                 checked and the answer is no", "we checked and something is in the way" and
#                 "nobody has checked" are four different states, and collapsing any of them
#                 loses exactly the information a later reader needs (#1591).
#   url           direct PDF URL, no credentials, no paid PACER; RECAP mirror where one exists
#   sha256        64 hex of the exact bytes, or `-` when the row is not `vetted`
#   source        court | agency | foia | sec | press
#   public_basis  why this document is lawfully public
#   truth_url     where the hidden value was PUBLISHED (tier B), or `-`
#                 An EXCLUSION must name the ground it rests on, and the grounds are:
#                   who it would expose   — victims, private individuals, minors
#                   what it still is      — sealed, under a protective order, SSI, classified
#                   how it may be fetched — terms of service, robots.txt
#                   whether it can be sourced — no verifiable, stable, durable or reputable URL
#                 UnredactionBenchManifestTests holds the same list. Add a ground to both
#                 rather than padding a row's prose until the gate matches it.
#   vetting       THE ASSESSMENT, not the verdict. Says what was checked and what was found,
#                 including for `excluded` rows, so a later reader can re-judge it.
# VETTING (all three must be yes for `vetted`)
#   1. tier B: the text under the redaction is already published by a reputable
#      outlet or the court; or tier C: the document is plainly public record.
#   2. Recovery would NOT identify private individuals or victims. This is a
#      hard exclusion and it outranks "but it is already posted somewhere".
#   3. The source's terms permit automated download.
#id
doj-epstein-2025-release
column9: EXCLUDED, and not because it is unavailable — it is posted and the files are exactly the failure modes this bench measures. Vetting question 2 fails: the redactions in this release cover victim and third-party names, so recovering them would identify the people the redaction exists to protect, and a bench that scores that recovery is doing the harm regardless of who reads the number. Question 1 also fails for tier B (no published ground truth) and the whole point of the release is that there is none. If this is ever revisited it is under #1603's value-free POSITIONAL design only — measure whether a mark leaks, never what it leaks — and that is a separate decision a human makes, not a status change here.

column1: manafort-2019-breach-response-471
column7: US federal court filing; federal court records are public domain (17 USC 105, Banks v. Manchester). Fetched from the RECAP mirror, never PACER.
column9: VETTED and VERIFIED, not assumed. (1) The hidden text was published the day it was filed and has been reported on continuously since. (2) No private individuals or victims: a convicted defendant, an indicted co-conspirator and a presidential campaign, all public figures in a public corruption matter. (3) storage.courtlistener.com serves no robots.txt (404, no restriction) and returned 200 to this bench's self-identifying User-Agent; the CourtListener web site itself 403s non-browser agents, so this row pins the storage URL and the script never scrapes the docket. Leak CONFIRMED without excise: pdftotext reads 46 word types present here and absent from the corrected entry 472, with zero the other way -- the containment signature of text removed there and left here -- and pdftocairo renders the bars. This document is why #1617 exists: excise reported 0 marks and 0 findings on it before that fix.

column1: manafort-2019-breach-response-472
column7: US federal court filing; public domain as above. Docketed the same day as 471 as the CORRECTED redacted version.
column9: VETTED as a NEGATIVE CONTROL, which is why it is tier C and carries no ground-truth pointer: it is the same brief with the redaction properly applied, so a correct unredact recovers NOTHING from it. That makes it the most valuable row in the file -- a pair that differs only in whether the redaction worked separates a real detector from an eager one, which no synthetic fixture can. Measured: 24 marks, 0 recovered, both before and after #1617, while its sibling went 0/0 to 25/24. Same vetting answers as 471 on all three questions.

column1: ftc-v-amazon-complaint-2023-09
column7: US government work, public domain (17 USC 105). FTC v. Amazon.com, No. 2:23-cv-01495-JHC (W.D. Wash.), published by the FTC on its own case page.
column9: BLOCKED, not rejected -- wanted, and the obstacle is mechanical. ftc.gov's robots.txt PERMITS this path (User-agent: *, Crawl-delay: 5, no Disallow on /system/files/), but its edge returns 403 to every self-identifying User-Agent tried from this host, including plain curl and two that name the bench. Getting the file would mean impersonating a browser, which contradicts the rule that this script identifies itself, so that is a call for a human rather than something to work around quietly; fetching by hand is trivial. Vetting otherwise clean: corporate conduct, no private individuals or victims, the only people named are executives named in a public government complaint. Paired with the November re-release below it is the strongest tier-B shape available -- the same complaint published twice by the same source with materially fewer redactions the second time, so ground truth is a file diff rather than a journalist's paraphrase.

column1: ftc-v-amazon-complaint-2023-11
column7: US government work, public domain (17 USC 105). The same complaint, re-published by the FTC on 2023-11-02 as 'Complaint [Public Redacted Version] [Redactions Updated]' with substantially fewer redactions.
column9: BLOCKED for the same 403 reason as its September sibling, and blocked rather than vetted for a second reason worth stating: the ground truth here is the LESS-redacted re-release, which means the truth_url would have to point at a file this manifest also lists, and the value itself belongs in the gitignored local ground-truth file, never here. Once a human clears the fetch this becomes the tier-B scoring pair. No private individuals or victims; robots.txt permits the path.

column1: tsa-screening-management-sop-2008
column7: Widely republished after a 2009 FedBizOpps posting; the original government host (FedBizOpps.gov) is decommissioned and SAM.gov did not retain it.
column9: EXCLUDED on two independent grounds, either sufficient. First, the content is Sensitive Security Information under 49 CFR Parts 15 and 1520 and every page carries the SSI marking; wide republication does not lift that designation, so a bench row here means deliberately recovering SSI. Second and more practical: no reputable primary host survives, and the three live copies are transparency-site mirrors of which at least one (Cryptome) follows a known practice of ANNOTATING the recovered text in clear -- fetching it would import the very values this bench exists never to hold. The mechanism it demonstrates is covered by synthetic fixtures. If someone wants it back it should return as a detector-only row with no recovery assertion, and that is a human's decision.

column1: nyt-nsa-2014-leaky-apps
column7: Published by The New York Times on 2014-01-27 in Snowden-archive reporting.
column9: EXCLUDED, hard, on vetting question 2. The recoverable text is reported to be the name of the individual NSA employee who authored the presentation, together with a targeted network identifier. That is a named working-level government employee, not a public figure, whose name was published by accident -- exactly the private-individual case the exclusion rule is written for, and it outranks the fact that the file is posted in several places. Also, no stable primary URL could be verified; the only reliably reachable copy is one that exists specifically to DISPLAY the recovered values, which disqualifies it as an input rather than recommending it. The mechanism is covered synthetically.

column1: ftc-v-meta-2025-opening-demonstratives
column7: Defense opening-statement demonstratives used in open court, FTC v. Meta Platforms, No. 1:20-cv-03590-JEB (D.D.C.), April 2025.
column9: EXCLUDED. Note the date: this is April 2025, not 2023. Two grounds. First, no verifiable stable URL exists -- trial demonstratives are not docketed, the FTC case page hosts only the FTC's own slides, and there is no RECAP entry to pin, so it fails the sourcing bar outright. Second, the concealed material is the trade secrets of THIRD PARTIES (Apple, Google, Snap) produced under a protective order and never unsealed, whose counsel objected on the record; 'already reported' is not a basis when the seal still stands and the objecting parties are not the ones who leaked it. Private individuals are not the issue here, which is why the rule needs reading as written rather than as a checklist.
